Mobile-VideoGPT: Fast and Accurate Video Understanding Language Model
Over the past decade, techniques such as knowledge dis-
tillation (Hinton et al., 2015; Romero et al., 2015), model
pruning (Han et al., 2016; He et al., 2017), efficient atten-
tion (Shaker et al., 2023; Maaz et al., 2022), and parameter-
efficient fine-tuning (Houlsby et al., 2019) have partially
addressed the challenge of reducing model complexity un-
der resource constraints. However, these strategies often
come with notable performance trade-offs or require spe-
cialized hardware accelerators. Moreover, while they may
effectively reduce the size of individual components (e.g.,
visual or text encoders), ensuring efficient projection and
integration across modalities for video understanding and
preserving advanced capabilities remains a challenge.
To this end, we introduce Mobile-VideoGPT, an efficient
video understanding language model that balances between
robust performance and high throughput for real-time per-
formance. We demonstrate the efficiency and the effective-
ness of Mobile-VideoGPT across multiple video conversa-
tion benchmarks, including ActivityNet-QA, EgoSchema,
MLVU, MVBench, NextQA, and PerceptionTest, where it
doesn’t only faster than the previous SoTA, but also outper-
forms them (See Figure 1). Our contributions in this work
are as follows:
1. A lightweight multimodal model designed specifically
for real-time video understanding. To our knowledge,
this work is the first work to propose a lightweight and
efficient video understanding framework with a focus
on real-time throughput.
2. We propose a novel frame scoring and selection strat-
egy that optimally selects the representative video key-
frames, along with efficient token projection, to en-
hance the model’s ability to maintain visual fidelity
while reducing computational overhead and allowing
for efficient video processing.
3. Our architecture is highly optimized for resource-
constrained environments, featuring a compact 1GB
model size and requiring only 3GB of VRAM. This
efficient design enables remarkable inference speeds
of 46 tokens per second on a single NVIDIA RTX
A6000 GPU, highlighting its suitability for real-time
applications.
4. Mobile-VideoGPT showcases superior performance
compared to competitive models across six video
understanding benchmarks, achieving an average
improvement of 6 points over LLaVA-OneVision-
0.5B (Li et al., 2024a). Our model is also 40% more
parameter-efficient and more than 2× higher through-
put, underscoring its effectiveness and practicality.
2. Related Work
Small Language Models (SLMs): In the past year, the
rise of large language models (LLMs) has driven signif-
icant progress in natural language processing, including
proprietary models like GPT-4 (OpenAI, 2023a), and open-
source models such as LLaMA (Touvron et al., 2023a)
and DeepSeek (Liu et al., 2024a). Although these mod-
els have sparked increased interest in enhancing the per-
formance of LLMs, the large size of these models often
leads to substantial memory consumption and slow process-
ing speeds. Moreover, the energy demands associated with
training and operating these models raise important sustain-
ability issues, which are becoming increasingly urgent as
LLMs expand in scale and complexity. To address this,
there has been a growing trend in the development of small
and medium-sized LLMs, such as Qwen2-0.5B (Yang et al.,
2024) and Llama3.2-1B (AI, 2024), specifically designed
for resource-constrained environments. Given the limited
computational capabilities of edge devices such as mobile
phones, autonomous vehicles, and embodied AI systems,
several lightweight LLMs (Li et al., 2023c; Zhang et al.,
2024a; Liu et al., 2024c; Chu et al., 2023) have gained signif-
icant attention. TinyLLaMA (Zhang et al., 2024a) conducts
great open-source work on their 1.1B base and chat models
with the same architecture and tokenizer as LLaMa2 (Tou-
vron et al., 2023b). MobileLLaMA (Chu et al., 2023) scales
down the architecture of LLaMA and releases 1B and 3B
models trained from scratch with public datasets. Recently,
MobileLLM (Liu et al., 2024c) optimizes sub-billion param-
eter models by proposing an immediate block-wise weight-
sharing approach. These compact models are optimized to
deliver efficient performance while addressing the unique
constraints of resource-limited environments. Another vital
line of research involves applying model compression tech-
niques for LLMs, such as pruning (Sun et al., 2024; Frantar
& Alistarh, 2023; Ma et al., 2023), quantization (Xiao et al.,
2023; Li et al., 2024d; Frantar et al., 2023), and low-rank
decomposition (Yao et al., 2024). These techniques reduce
the computational demands of LLMs and enhance their prac-
ticality for deployment on resource-constrained devices.
Vision Language Models: The advancement of visual lan-
guage models (VLMs) has been significantly shaped by
the introduction of CLIP (Radford et al., 2021), which uti-
lizes a contrastive loss to align vision and language em-
beddings within a unified representation space. Recent
progress in LLMs has further enhanced the development of
VLMs, as demonstrated in Kosmos-2 (Peng et al., 2023),
GLaMM (Rasheed et al., 2024), BLIP-2 (Li et al., 2023a),
MiniGPT-4 (Zhu et al., 2024), LLaVA (Liu et al., 2023b) and
PALO (Rasheed et al., 2025). These models combine visual
and linguistic features, leveraging advanced cross-modal de-
signs, such as cross-attention mechanisms, Q-Former mod-
ules, or simple multi-layer perceptron (MLP) layers.
Video Language Models: Current video understanding
models typically rely on either image (Li et al., 2023b;
Ataallah et al., 2024; Lin et al., 2023b) or video en-

coders (Maaz et al., 2024b) to process visual inputs in
conjunction with advanced LLMs. Image encoders excel at
capturing rich spatial details from frame sequences but often
lack the explicit temporal context critical for understanding
intricate action sequences in videos. On the other hand,
video encoders provide the necessary temporal context but
are frequently limited by computational constraints, leading
to the processing of only sparse frames at lower resolutions
and consequently reducing both contextual and spatial un-
derstanding. VideoMamba (Li et al., 2024b) is a recent
parameter-efficient video encoder that addresses the dual
challenges of local redundancy and global dependencies in
video tasks by adaptively extending the Mamba architec-
ture to the video domain, it employs a linear-complexity
operator for efficient long-term modeling and achieves a
balance between performance and scalability. Early efforts
such as Video-ChatGPT (Maaz et al., 2024a) and Video-
LLaMA (Zhang et al., 2023) have expanded image-based
models into the video domain by integrating components
specifically designed to capture temporal features. In these
models, frame-level visual features are processed by vision
encoders with pooling techniques and fed into LLMs. Gold-
fish (Ataallah et al., 2024) and VideoGPT+ (Maaz et al.,
2024b) segment videos into short clips and process each
clip independently to enhance efficiency and scalability for
the long videos. LLAVA-OneVision (Li et al., 2024a) builds
upon these advancements by introducing a unified frame-
work that can effectively handle both image and video tasks.
Unlike prior methods that rely on separate encoders for dis-
tinct modalities, LLAVA-OneVision utilizes a single vision
encoder designed to seamlessly extract frame-level features,
while the temporal understanding is learned through the
position embedding of the language model.
Although the above methods demonstrate impressive per-
formance in video-language understanding, they remain
impractical for deployment on edge devices due to their
high computational demands, large memory footprints, and
dependency on powerful hardware accelerators. They of-
ten rely on complex architectures with large vision and
language encoders, and large input resolution, requiring
significant GPU and storage resources to handle real-time
video processing, while the edge environments have limited
processing power. These limitations motivate our work on
Mobile-VideoGPT, which seeks to develop a lightweight,
resource-efficient video understanding model capable of
running on edge devices by optimizing model size, reducing
memory usage, and enabling real-time inference without
sacrificing performance.

We introduce the Mobile-VideoGPT framework, specifically
designed for efficient video understanding. It incorporates
both an image encoder and a video encoder; each optimized
for speed and number of parameters, along with compact,
efficient projection modules that project the latent visual
features into a suitable format for the small yet powerful
language model.

2024), Mobile-VideoGPT adopts a dual-encoder design

trated in Figure 2, the proposed framework consists of: (1) a

ing spatial and semantic features, (2) a lightweight Video-
Mamba encoder (Li et al., 2024b) for extracting temporal
information, (3) an Efficient Token Projection (ETProj) mod-
ule for feature reduction and projection, and (4) an SLM for
generating context-rich textual responses.

Fclip ∈R T × Hs × Ws × Ds,

Fvmamba ∈R K × Ht × Wt × Dt,
where Ht and Wt represent spatial dimensions for the video

Next, both the clip-based embeddings and the VideoMamba
embeddings are processed through Efficient Token Projec-
tion modules. Concretely, ETProj reduces and transforms
each modality into a unified vision–language embedding

3.4. Model Architecture
The SLM is designed as a compact 1B model with 3GB

small variant of GPT-1, scaled down to 0.5B parameters
with 3GB of VRAM, and optimized for efficient token
projection and inference speed. The architecture includes a
small transformer with 6 layers and 6 attention heads,

We evaluate the model on six video benchmarks, including
ActivityNet-QA, EgoSchema, MLVU, MVBench, NextQA,
and PerceptionTest. The results are shown in Figure 1 and
Table 1. On each benchmark, Mobile-VideoGPT achieves an
average improvement of 6 points over the baseline models,
with a 40% reduction in parameters and a 2x increase in
throughput compared to the baseline. The model achieves an
average inference speed of 46 tokens per second on a single
NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPU.

signs, such as cross-attention mechanisms, Q-Former mod-
ules, or simple multi-layer perceptron (MLP) layers.
Video Language Models: Current video understanding
models typically rely on either image (Li et al., 2023b;
Ataallah et al., 2024; Lin et al., 2023b) or video en-
2

Mobile-VideoGPT: Fast and Accurate Video Understanding Language Model
coders (Maaz et al., 2024b) to process visual inputs in
conjunction with advanced LLMs. Image encoders excel at
capturing rich spatial details from frame sequences but often
lack the explicit temporal context critical for understanding
intricate action sequences in videos. On the other hand,
video encoders provide the necessary temporal context but
are frequently limited by computational constraints, leading
to the processing of only sparse frames at lower resolutions
and consequently reducing both contextual and spatial un-
derstanding. VideoMamba (Li et al., 2024b) is a recent
parameter-efficient video encoder that addresses the dual
challenges of local redundancy and global dependencies in
video tasks by adaptively extending the Mamba architec-
ture to the video domain, it employs a linear-complexity
operator for efficient long-term modeling and achieves a
balance between performance and scalability. Early efforts
such as Video-ChatGPT (Maaz et al., 2024a) and Video-
LLaMA (Zhang et al., 2023) have expanded image-based
models into the video domain by integrating components
specifically designed to capture temporal features. In these
models, frame-level visual features are processed by vision
encoders with pooling techniques and fed into LLMs. Gold-
fish (Ataallah et al., 2024) and VideoGPT+ (Maaz et al.,
2024b) segment videos into short clips and process each
clip independently to enhance efficiency and scalability for
the long videos. LLAVA-OneVision (Li et al., 2024a) builds
upon these advancements by introducing a unified frame-
work that can effectively handle both image and video tasks.
Unlike prior methods that rely on separate encoders for dis-
tinct modalities, LLAVA-OneVision utilizes a single vision
encoder designed to seamlessly extract frame-level features,
while the temporal understanding is learned through the
position embedding of the language model.
Although the above methods demonstrate impressive per-
formance in video-language understanding, they remain
impractical for deployment on edge devices due to their
high computational demands, large memory footprints, and
dependency on powerful hardware accelerators. They of-
ten rely on complex architectures with large vision and
language encoders, and large input resolution, requiring
significant GPU and storage resources to handle real-time
video processing, while the edge environments have limited
processing power. These limitations motivate our work on
Mobile-VideoGPT, which seeks to develop a lightweight,
resource-efficient video understanding model capable of
running on edge devices by optimizing model size, reducing
memory usage, and enabling real-time inference without
sacrificing performance.
3. Mobile-VideoGPT
We introduce the Mobile-VideoGPT framework, specifically
designed for efficient video understanding. It incorporates
both an image encoder and a video encoder; each optimized
for speed and number of parameters, along with compact,
efficient projection modules that project the latent visual
features into a suitable format for the small yet powerful
language model.
3.1. Overall Architectural Design
Inspired by recent work (Maaz et al., 2024b; Zohar et al.,
2024), Mobile-VideoGPT adopts a dual-encoder design
combined with a small language model (SLM). As illus-
trated in Figure 2, the proposed framework consists of: (1) a
CLIP-based image encoder (Radford et al., 2021) for captur-
ing spatial and semantic features, (2) a lightweight Video-
Mamba encoder (Li et al., 2024b) for extracting temporal
information, (3) an Efficient Token Projection (ETProj) mod-
ule for feature reduction and projection, and (4) an SLM for
generating context-rich textual responses.
We start by uniformly sampling T frames from the input
video. For each frame t ∈{1, . . . , T}, we extract spatial

Fclip ∈R T × Hs × Ws × Ds,
where Hs and Ws denote the spatial dimensions for image

encoder-M to encode the temporal features. This yields
Fvmamba ∈R K × Ht × Wt × Dt,
where Ht and Wt represent spatial dimensions for the video
features, and Dt is the temporal feature depth.
Next, both the clip-based embeddings and the VideoMamba
embeddings are processed through Efficient Token Projec-

4.1. Implementation Details
In our experiments, we utilize CLIP-B/16 (Radford et al.,
2021) as the image encoder and VideoMamba-M (Li et al.,
2024b) as the video encoder, alongside the Qwen-2.5,
0.5/1.5B (Yang et al., 2024) LLM. Both image and video
encoders process inputs at a resolution of 224 × 224. Our
training pipeline consists of two warm-up phases followed
by an instruction-tuning phase. During warm-up, we sepa-
rately train with the image and video encoders on the CC-
595K dataset (Liu et al., 2023a), optimizing only the vision-
to-language adapters while keeping the remaining model
parameters frozen. In the instruction-tuning phase, we apply
LoRA (Hu et al., 2022) with a rank of r = 64 to the LLM,
while the vision-to-language adapters are fully trained and
the vision encoders remain frozen. The learning rate is set
to 1e−3 during warm-up and 2e−4 during instruction tuning.
During instruction tuning, we first sample videos at 1 FPS,
followed by a uniform sampling of 16 frames. The value of
K is set to 8 for attention-based frame scoring.
We use instruction-tuning data from VideoGPT+ (Maaz
et al., 2024b), which consists of Kinetics-710 (Kay et al.,
2017), Something-Something-v2 (Goyal et al., 2017), con-
versations from VideoChat (Li et al., 2023b), CLEVRER (Yi
et al., 2019), the VQA dataset from WebVid (Bain et al.,
2021), and NExT-QA (Xiao et al., 2021), along with the Per-
ceptionTest (P˘atr˘aucean et al., 2023) subset from LLaVA-
178K (Zhang et al., 2024c) and a subset of VideoChat2-
IT (Li et al., 2024c). The instruction-tuning dataset amounts
to approx. 1M samples, and we train our model for two
epochs. Although we use only a fraction of the instruction-
tuning dataset compared to previous SoTA approaches
(e.g., LLaVA-OneVision, which utilizes approx. 4.8M
instruction-tuning samples combining images, multi-image,
and videos), our novel frame-selection algorithm, along
with the carefully designed training recipe for the efficient
MLLM architecture, results in superior performance.

video MLLMs across 20 temporal understanding sub-tasks,

Notably, our model performs well in tasks requiring strong
temporal reasoning. For example, in the Moving Direc-
tion category, our 0.5B model scores 59.0%, significantly
higher than the second-best score of 31.0% by LLaVA-Mini.
Similar trends are observed in Action Localization, Ac-
tion Count, Moving Count, Moving Attribute, and State
Change sub-tasks. We attribute this strong performance to
our attention-based frame selection algorithm coupled with
the video encoder, which effectively captures video-specific
dependencies. However, our model performs less effectively
on fine-grained tasks, likely due to lower input resolution
and the limited number of frames we use to maintain the
efficiency of our design with real-time processing.

except for MLVU, where the video-encoder-only design
performs best. Overall, these results highlight the advan-
tage of the dual-encoder design in capturing spatiotemporal
features, leading to improved video understanding.
To evaluate the effectiveness of our frame-selection algo-
rithm, we train the model without frame selection, meaning
the video encoder processes all frames, leading to lower
throughput. The results show that our attention-based frame-
selection algorithm performs on-bar by processing all video

4.4. Qualitative Results
Figure 4 compares the qualitative results of our Mobile-
Video GPT with two recent baseline models (LLaVa-Mini-
8B (Zhang et al., 2025) and LLaVa-OneVision-0.5B (Li
et al., 2024a)) on two video segments: a nighttime field
hockey game (top) and a skateboarding session (bottom).
The baseline models offer incomplete or generic descrip-
tions and miss important details, such as the final score
in the hockey game. In contrast, our Mobile-Video GPT
accurately captures the entire temporal progression with
detailed descriptions. Notably, the figure also highlights
our model’s significantly higher throughput (over 40 tokens
per second) with lower latency. Mobile-VideoGPT-0.5B is
2–3× faster than LLaVa-OneVision-0.5B and 5× faster than
LLaVa-Mini in the top video, and more than 10× faster in
the bottom video. These findings demonstrate the efficiency
of our method for real-time video understanding tasks and
underscore the robustness and speed of Mobile-Video GPT
in diverse scenarios.
